analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. greenhouse gas pollution 80% below 1990 levels by 2050, with vehicle, power plant, and renewable electricity standards.
analysis.headline: Twenty senators backed the bill, but it never received a hearing, markup, or vote in two years and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to require the EPA to cut U.S. global warming pollution back to 1990 levels by 2020 and 80% below 1990 levels by 2050, roughly 2% per year through 2020. It set emission limits on new cars starting in model year 2016 and on power plants, required electricity suppliers to get 20% of power from renewables by 2020 and to hit yearly energy-efficiency targets, and required companies to disclose climate risks to investors. Emission allowances could have been given to households and communities hurt by the transition.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to climate-related damage: households, coastal communities, farmers, and future generations. The bill also let the EPA allocate emission allowances to households, communities, and workers hit hard by the shift away from fossil fuels, and would have benefited renewable energy and efficiency businesses that gain guaranteed markets under the electricity standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, renewable energy firms, and future generations

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the EPA to promulgate rules returning U.S. emissions to 1990 levels by 2020, through reductions of roughly 2% per year from 2010 to 2020, and to 80% below 1990 levels by 2050, with a goal of keeping global temperature rise under 2 degrees Celsius.

Beginning in model year 2016, each manufacturer's car fleet had to average no more than 205 grams of CO2-equivalent per mile for smaller cars, with limits for larger vehicles and heavy trucks from 2020.

Electric generation units starting after 2011 would have had to meet an emission standard no higher than a new combined-cycle natural gas plant, and by 2030 every power plant regardless of age would have had to meet that standard.

Retail electricity suppliers would have had to get 5% of power from renewables by 2008, rising to 20% by 2020, and to hit annual energy-efficiency and peak-demand reduction targets or pay a fee of at least 4 cents per kilowatt-hour.

The EPA could have allocated emission allowances to households, communities, and companies hit with disproportionate harm from the transition to a lower-carbon economy, with proceeds distributed to the beneficiaries.

Public companies would have had to disclose to investors their financial exposure from their own emissions and from global warming's economic impacts, with the SEC treating global warming as a known trend.
It was the sense of the Senate that federal funding for clean, low-carbon energy research and deployment should increase at least 100% each year for ten years.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies, coal- and oil-fired power plants, oil refiners, and other major emitters, who would have faced emission limits, a low-carbon fuel mandate, and credit-trading obligations. Energy consumers, especially in coal-dependent regions, would have borne some higher energy prices during the transition, which the bill tried to soften by allowing allowances to flow to hard-hit households and communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and utilities that emit heavily

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledged that the transition could cause disproportionate harm: it allowed the EPA to allocate allowances to communities, individuals, and companies that suffered adverse impacts from the shift to a lower-carbon economy, an implicit admission that energy prices and fossil-fuel-dependent regions would bear real costs.

The market-based program included a 'technology-indexed stop price' under which the emissions cap could freeze for up to three years whenever the price of emission allowances exceeded the cost of deploying clean technology, potentially delaying reductions when they were most expensive.

If the National Academy of Sciences determined any requirement technologically infeasible, the EPA could adjust or delay power plant standards, the low-carbon generation schedule, and vehicle standards, giving industry a science-verified exit ramp from the strictest mandates.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that cutting economy-wide emissions roughly 2% per year would have raised electricity and fuel costs for years, and that the bill's design left the exact burden on consumers uncertain because it delegated allocation of allowances to the EPA.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill paired the most aggressive emission targets of any Senate climate bill of that Congress with explicit escape valves: allowance price floors that could pause the cap, and National Academy determinations that could delay standards as infeasible. The costs would have fallen early and concretely on coal regions and energy bills, while the benefits—avoided climate damage, cleaner air, fuel savings from efficient vehicles—accrue broadly and over decades. The household allowance provision was meant to offset consumer costs, but its details were left entirely to future EPA rules, so how well ordinary people would have been protected depends on regulations never written.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Global Warming Pollution Reduction Act on January 16, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The record shows no committee action after referral; the only later entries are sponsor introductory remarks in June 2007, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever appears in the action history.
Nineteen Senate Democrats joined Sanders as cosponsors; no Republican did.

The bill's centerpiece was a mandatory EPA program cutting U.S. emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 and 80% below 1990 levels by 2050, alongside vehicle, power plant, renewable electricity, and efficiency standards.
The 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and heavily emitting utilities were better off, since no mandatory emission limits took effect. The 20 cosponsoring senators also avoided ever having to cast a recorded vote on climate policy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal and oil interests; no vote ever happened

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Global Warming Pollution Reduction Act and delivered introductory remarks in January and June 2007.

for.name: 19 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Boxer, Kennedy, Menendez, Lautenberg, Leahy, Reed, Akaka, Inouye, Feingold, and Whitehouse.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer (D), an original cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the remaining two years of the Congress.

against.name: Fossil fuel and electric utility interests
against.role: Major emitters facing the bill's caps and mandates
against.what_they_did: Fought mandatory economy-wide emission limits during the 2007-2008 climate debate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, but the support that existed was entirely on one side of the aisle: Sanders and 19 Senate Democrats cosponsored, and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: New power plants would have had to match the emission rate of a gas plant, all plants by 2030, and coal generators would have faced low-carbon generation quotas with penalties. Coal interests' preference for no limits ran against the public's interest in cutting emissions.

The bill capped emissions economy-wide, set vehicle emission standards from model year 2016, and required 5 billion gallons of low-carbon renewable fuel in gasoline annually from 2015. Industry resistance to emission limits ran against the public's interest in reduced pollution.

A 20% renewable electricity requirement by 2020, binding efficiency targets, and doubled clean-energy research funding would have created guaranteed markets. Their gains coincide with the public's emission reductions and lower energy waste.

Manufacturers would have faced binding fleet emission limits starting in model year 2016, with compliance costs passed partly into prices, but the same standards produce fuel savings for drivers and cleaner air. Academy infeasibility findings gave the EPA flexibility to adjust requirements.

The bill set the ceiling for new fossil generation at the emission rate of a combined-cycle natural gas plant, giving gas a structural advantage over coal. That substitution also serves the emission-reduction goal.
